About me

Marieui Karagianni, psychologist MSc

I believe in therapy with a clear structure and a scientific basis — one that always starts from the person: your pace, your needs, what matters to you.

I am a licensed psychologist – psychotherapist. I studied Psychology at Panteion University, where I also completed my master’s degree in Applied Cognitive and Developmental Psychology. I am training in Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Adults at the Society for Cognitive Behavioural Studies.

I work with adults in individual sessions — at my practice in Ilioupoli and online — and with parents who want to support their child better. I collaborate with the Trust Your Therapist and Mind Your Emotion initiatives, and for three years I worked at a support centre for children, teenagers and adults.

My first clinical experience was at the Psychiatric Department of Evangelismos General Hospital in Athens and on the 10306 psychosocial support line. I also take part in research: in 2024 the British Journal of Developmental Psychology published a study on Theory of Mind and creativity that I co-authored.

Services

Psychotherapy for what weighs on you

Individual sessions for adults and counselling for parents — at the practice in Ilioupoli or online, 50 minutes each.

Anxiety & stress

When anxiety never switches off

Anxiety is a natural signal of the body; it becomes a problem when it stays switched on all day — a tight chest, racing thoughts, sleep that doesn’t rest you, tension spilling into work and relationships. In our sessions we map together what triggers your anxiety, which thoughts inflate it and what you do to avoid it. Then we work with practical tools from cognitive behavioural therapy: breathing and relaxation, re-examining thoughts, organising your time, gradually facing what you avoid. The goal is not to never feel anxious, but for anxiety to stop making your decisions.

  • Generalised anxiety
  • Work stress
  • Sleep & tension
Talk to me about it

Panic attacks

The wave that seems to sweep you away

A panic attack often comes “out of nowhere”: a racing heart, breathlessness, dizziness, numbness, the feeling that you are losing control or that something serious is happening in your body. It is a frightening experience but — once a medical cause has been ruled out — it is not dangerous, and it can be treated. First we understand how it works: how a bodily sensation is read as danger and how fear feeds the symptoms. Then you learn to recognise them, to stay with the wave without fighting it and, step by step, to return to the places and activities you started to avoid.

  • Panic disorder
  • Agoraphobia
  • Fear of the symptoms
Talk to me about it

Phobias

A world that grows again

Fear of heights, flying, animals, enclosed spaces, injections or driving can make your world smaller, bit by bit. Phobias respond very well to cognitive behavioural therapy. We work with gradual exposure: together we build a “ladder” from the least to the most difficult and climb it one step at a time, at your own pace and never by surprise. At the same time we look at the thoughts that keep the fear alive, so that the change does not stay in the therapy room but carries on into your everyday life.

  • Specific phobias
  • Social anxiety
  • Gradual exposure
Talk to me about it

OCD

Breaking the obsessive cycle

Thoughts that keep coming back although you don’t want them, and actions you feel you “must” do to calm down: checking, washing, counting, arranging, mental rituals. OCD is exhausting, because every bit of relief is short-lived and the cycle starts again. In therapy we understand how the obsession – compulsion cycle works and break it gradually with exposure and response prevention, a core technique of cognitive behavioural therapy. The work is done with respect, without rushing, with goals we set together — and with one steady aim: to win back the time and calm the cycle takes from you.

  • Checking & cleaning
  • Intrusive thoughts
  • Exposure & response prevention
Talk to me about it

Low mood

When nothing feels the way it used to

When sadness lasts for weeks, when nothing gives you pleasure the way it used to, when tiredness and withdrawal become everyday life, it is worth talking to someone. In our sessions there is room for whatever you feel, without judgement, and we look for the small, concrete steps that bring movement back: activities that fill you up, routine, contact with your people. We also look at your inner dialogue — the harsh, sweeping thoughts that weigh your mood down — and learn to weigh them more fairly. Where needed, working alongside a psychiatrist is arranged together with you.

  • Mood disorders
  • Sadness & distress
  • Behavioural activation
Talk to me about it

Self-esteem

Seeing yourself more fairly

The inner voice that says “I am not enough” shapes how we work, how we love and how much we dare. It often comes with perfectionism, difficulty saying “no” and fear of other people’s judgement. In therapy we find where these beliefs come from and how they are kept going today, and we try out new ways of relating to yourself in practice: with more understanding, realistic goals and respect for your limits. As one client put it, the aim is “to see myself with more kindness”.

  • Perfectionism
  • Boundaries & assertiveness
  • Self-image
Talk to me about it

Parent counselling

Support for you, so you can support your child

When a child — young, teenage or even adult — is struggling, parents often feel helpless, guilty or afraid of doing the wrong thing. Parent counselling is a space for you: we understand what your child is going through, how it affects the family and what you can do in practice — how to talk, how to set limits, how to support without unintentionally feeding the anxiety. My work at a support centre for children, teenagers and adults and my master’s in Developmental Psychology give me a clear picture of every age.

  • Children & teens
  • Adult children
  • Limits & communication
Talk to me about it

How anxiety works

Why avoidance keeps anxiety alive

A simple chart we often use in cognitive behavioural therapy. Choose what you do when anxiety rises — then keep scrolling.

Something triggers anxiety — a place, a thought, a sensation in the body. The curve rises.

You leave, or do something to calm down. Relief comes at once…

…but the brain keeps the lesson “I was safe because I escaped”. Next time anxiety starts higher.

An illustrative chart; in therapy, exposure is always gradual and at your own pace.

How we start

Four simple steps

  1. 1

    You call

    A short chat about what is on your mind and whether you prefer the practice in Ilioupoli or online.

  2. 2

    Getting to know you

    In the first session I listen to your story and we understand together what is happening — no rush and no labels.

  3. 3

    A shared plan

    We set goals that matter to you and agree how we will work and how often we will meet.

  4. 4

    Tools for life

    You try out in daily life what we work on in session — and the tools stay yours after therapy ends.

Questions

Frequently asked questions

Can’t find your question? Call — it is the simplest way to ask.

What is cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)?

It is an evidence-based form of psychotherapy that looks at how our thoughts, feelings and behaviours are connected. It is structured and goal-focused: we set goals together, you learn practical tools and try them out in daily life. It has strong research support for anxiety, panic attacks, phobias, obsessive-compulsive disorder and depression.

How long is a session and how often do we meet?

Each session lasts 50 minutes. We usually meet once a week, especially at the beginning, so there is continuity; later on sessions can become less frequent. We always decide the frequency together, based on your needs and your schedule. Sessions take place at the practice in Ilioupoli or online.

How many sessions will I need?

There is no single number for everyone. CBT is often shorter than other approaches, but the length depends on what is troubling you, how long it has been there and what your goals are. In the first meetings we discuss a realistic timeframe and review it together as we go.

Do you offer online sessions?

Yes, sessions also take place online by video call, so we can work together from anywhere in Greece or abroad. All you need is a quiet corner where you cannot be overheard, an internet connection and a phone or computer with a camera. The structure and length are the same as sessions at the practice.

Where is the practice?

The practice is on Kerkyras Street in Ilioupoli, Athens, near Iroon Polytechneiou Avenue. It is easy to reach from Ilioupoli, Agios Dimitrios, Argyroupoli and Vyronas. You will receive the exact address when your appointment is confirmed.

What happens in the first session?

The first session is about getting to know each other. You tell me what brings you, how long it has been bothering you and what you would like to change; I explain how I work and answer your questions. You don’t need to prepare anything or know in advance “what you have”. At the end we decide together whether and how to continue.

What are the symptoms of a panic attack?

Symptoms vary from person to person; the most common are a racing heart, sweating, trembling, breathlessness, chest pain, dizziness, numbness or tingling and chills. Sometimes you or the world around you feel strange or distant. They come with a sense of losing control or a fear of dying. If you experience them for the first time, see a doctor first to rule out a physical cause.

Can I come as a parent, without my child?

Yes. Parent counselling is for the parents themselves — one or both of you can come, without the child. We talk about what you notice, how it affects you and concrete ways to support your child day to day, whether they are young, a teenager or an adult.

How do I pay?

You can pay by card or in cash. If you need to cancel or move your appointment, please let me know as early as possible.

Is what we discuss confidential?

Yes. Everything we discuss in sessions is confidential and protected by the psychologists’ code of ethics. The only exceptions provided by law concern a serious risk to your life or the lives of others — and we talk about them openly from the very first meeting.
